title: A Jacobian determinant and condition heat map: where is the map singular or ill-conditioned?
summary: Two heat maps of a map's local behaviour: the determinant, which says how areas scale and where orientation flips, and the condition number, which says how lopsided the local stretch is. Singular places (fold curves) show as amber contours.

media.alt: Two square heat maps. Left: determinant with a rose centre, teal edges and an amber closed curve where it equals zero. Right: condition number on a logarithmic dark-purple to yellow scale, dark in the middle and bright near the same amber curve.
media.caption: Reference render of class F2.3 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: Where is the map singular or ill-conditioned?
read_the_figure.data: det J, cond J on grid
read_the_figure.axes: Both panels: x and y in the plane, equal scale, -1.2 to 1.2. Left colour: det J on a diverging scale centred on 1 (grey = area kept), rose below, teal above. Right colour: cond J on a logarithmic scale from 1 to about 30000. Amber: det J = 0, in both panels.
look_at: Where does det J cross zero? Follow the amber curve and note the sign inside.
Is the condition number large near the amber curve? Why?
Where is the map closest to an area-preserving, isotropic map (det J = 1, cond = 1)?
Which colour on the left means 'zero'? It is not the grey centre.
as_drawn: The map is (x, y) goes to (x + 0.9 sin 1.5y, y + 0.9 sin 1.5x). det J = 1 - 1.82 cos(1.5x) cos(1.5y), from -0.82 at the origin to 1.41 at the edge midpoints.
The scale of the left panel is centred on 1, so grey means area kept, not zero. The zero level sits in the rose half and is drawn by the amber contour.
At the origin cond J is 6.7 (dark purple). It rises steeply toward the amber curve; at the crossing (0.66, 0) it exceeds 10^5, beyond the colour bar's top at about 3 x 10^4, a grid-resolution limit.
read_the_figure.proves: Where the local map fails to be invertible (det J = 0) and where small errors in x, y are amplified most when going back from image to domain. It does not prove the global map is one-to-one.
if_wrong: A diverging colour map centred on zero for det J when the interesting value is 1: the neutral colour misleads.
A linear colour scale for the condition number: a few extreme pixels turn the rest black.
No singular contour: you cannot tell where the sign changes.

terms.meaning: Local area scale factor of the map; its sign tells orientation.
A point where det J = 0: the map is locally not invertible; it collapses a direction.
The stretch factors of the Jacobian along its two principal directions; the largest and smallest.
The ratio of largest to smallest singular value: the worst amplification of relative error, 1 for a pure rotation or scaling.
A colour map with a neutral middle and two hues for above and below it.
Very large condition number: tiny input changes cause huge output changes.

remember: det J = 0 means singular; det J < 0 means orientation is reversed.
cond J >= 1; cond = 1 only for similarity maps; cond is infinite where det J = 0.
Centre the diverging scale on the value that matters, and say which it is.
Use a log scale for cond.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Colour encodes a number at every point of the plane. On the left, hue (rose or teal) shows below or above 1 and lightness shows how far. On the right, a sequential scale on a log axis encodes the condition number. The amber contour is a line mark at det J = 0 repeated in both panels so the reader can compare them.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: The Jacobian is the local linear map; its determinant is the area scale and its condition number measures how unequally it stretches directions. Mapping both over the plane turns a question about a formula into a picture of where trouble lives. Putting the zero contour in both shows that the condition number blows up exactly where the determinant vanishes.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A diverging scale centred on 1 makes grey mean 'area kept', which differs from the more common 'grey = zero'. A linear scale for the condition number would be dominated by the huge values near the fold. Finite-difference Jacobians on a coarse grid underestimate extremes. And condition number alone does not say which direction is bad (use ellipse glyphs, F2.7).

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: A diverging scale centred on 1 or 0 puts the neutral colour where the reader expects meaning. A log scale for the condition number keeps both the near-isotropic region and the near-singular region visible. Both choices must be stated on the colour bar; this render does.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: To see directions use metric ellipses (F2.7). To see the grid use a deformed grid (F2.2). To see singular values separately, plot both as two maps. To find folds only, plot the contour det J = 0 alone.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add the fold contour in a heavier line and write the sign of the determinant inside it. Add a third panel for sigma_min, so the reader can see what is being squeezed.

steps.title: The Jacobian determinant
steps.note: At the origin det J = 1 - 1.8225 = -0.82. On the axis y = 0 it is zero where cos 1.5x = 0.549, so x = 0.66: the amber curve crosses the x axis there.

steps.title: Condition number
steps.note: At the origin J = [[1, 1.35], [1.35, 1]] has singular values 2.35 and 0.35, so kappa = 6.7 even though |det J| = 0.82: the determinant alone does not say how lopsided the stretch is. Approaching the fold sigma_min goes to zero, so kappa goes to infinity.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) where is the map singular? (2) What is the sign of det J inside the amber curve? (3) Is the condition number large at the centre?

solution.text: Along the amber curve. It crosses the x axis near x = 0.66 and the y axis near y = 0.66.
Rose inside: det J is negative there, down to -0.82 at the origin, so the map reverses orientation in the middle: the grid is folded over.
No: the centre is dark purple, cond about 6.7. The singular values are 2.35 and 0.35. The condition number only becomes huge close to the amber curve.

worked.answer: Singular on the amber curve (|x|, |y| about 0.66 on the axes); orientation reversed inside; condition number 6.7 at the centre, unbounded at the curve.

analyze.q: Why does the condition number grow without bound at the amber curve even though det J there is simply zero?
The determinant is -0.82 at the centre and cond is only 6.7. Explain why a large |det J| mismatch with 1 is not the same as ill-conditioning.
What would the left panel look like if the colour scale were centred on 0?

evaluate.q: A solver reports 'Jacobian is non-singular everywhere' based on det J > 0.001 on a coarse grid. How would you check more carefully?
evaluate.hint: Resolution, and condition number, not only determinant.

create: Draw the singular-value maps sigma_max and sigma_min instead and show where each is small.
Plot cond J along the line y = 0 on a log y axis and mark the fold.

checks.q: What does a negative determinant mean?
checks.answer: The map reverses orientation (a fold or reflection): the grid is flipped locally.

checks.q: A Jacobian has singular values 5 and 0.05. What is the condition number and what does it mean for inverting?
checks.answer: 100; relative errors can be amplified by up to a factor of 100 when inverting the map.

checks.q: det J and cond J are both plotted. Where could you have det J = 1 and still have a bad condition number?
checks.hint: Product versus ratio of singular values.
checks.answer: Singular values 10 and 0.1: determinant 1 but cond 100. Area is preserved while directions are stretched very unequally.
